#2015. Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell

Sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources. After claiming the first pole of his Formula One career, an absolutely stunning effort in his 192nd attempt – edging out Mercedes’ George Russell right at the death – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly revealed that a harmless jibe from his performance coach Ben Thorpe just before the session started had riled him up.

It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.

“Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference. “There are a few of us in the paddock who are. So we have exchanged our IDs on Chess.com and we have had a little game going on.

“I won yesterday, and another one that carried on into today,” the Frenchman added. “I was feeling confident and I was picking [taking] piece after piece. Then Ben told me: ‘You are getting George here but he is going to get you in a few minutes!’. And I thought ‘F--- off!’.”

What a way to break your duck. And what a day on which to do it. On Friday, Gasly lost his only podium of the season when the International Court of Appeal reinstated two five-second penalties he received in Monaco, dropping him from third to seventh in that race. The ruling produced fireworks when Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive adviser, then accused one of the judges on the ICA panel of being biased towards McLaren, one of two teams who had brought the appeal.

Another 24 hours later, the fireworks were for all the right reasons. And there was no appealing the result; the start of Russell’s final lap in Q3 was slightly compromised by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, but the Englishman could have no real complaints, losing out by 0.060secs in the end, prompting wild celebrations in the Alpine garage.

To say the result was a surprise would be an understatement. This was the Enstone team’s first pole in 17 years, since Fernando Alonso took P1 Renault at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

The warning signs were there. Alpine had been quick all weekend. But the Tifosi packing Monza’s grandstands fully expected it to be a battle between Mercedes and their beloved Ferrari for pole.

The Scuderia’s performance was underwhelming. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, the latter squeaking into Q3 by one thousandth of a second from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto. “F--- me,” Hamilton said after dodging that bullet.

And although they improved a bit in Q3, Hamilton managing to claim P5, just behind Leclerc in P4, they never threatened the front row. In fact, they later got lucky as McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who took P3, was later hit with a three-place grid drop post-qualifying for impeding Liam Lawson, meaning both Ferrari drivers rose one place.

It could prove significant. Hamilton, like Russell, knows this weekend represents a golden opportunity to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the title race. The two Britons are tied second in the championship heading into the weekend, 59 points behind the Italian. But Antonelli, who sacrificed his qualifying to help Russell, must start from the back of the grid on Sunday due to exceeding the permitted number of engines in a season.

It promises to be a fascinating race, with Antonelli fighting his way through the pack and Russell and Hamilton trying to make hay while they can. Russell sounded confident. “I think they [Alpine] have got a car that’s got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race. But, yeah, confident I’ve got the pace to go for the win.”

Could he be underestimating Gasly again? The Frenchman, who lives locally in Milan and speaks fluent Italian, has won here before. He claimed the only victory of his F1 career at Monza for AlphaTauri in 2020.

“Anything is possible tomorrow,” insisted Steve Nielsen, Alpine’s managing director. “We didn’t expect to be in pole position, we are. Tomorrow, good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let’s try to win it.”

Gasly himself said he had no idea what he was capable of. “My plan is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.” Perhaps that will be enough for another checkmate.

Antonelli acknowledged that his engine-parts grid penalty meant he had no reason not to assist his teamate Russell by offering towing assistance.

He seemed a little peeved at times on the radio, but he did his job. With Russell likely to need to return the favour for him later this season, there is no point causing bother.

He told Sky Sports: “It’s what I have to do. The team asked me and of course I did what I had to do, I tried to help as much as possible. It’s a bit weird going in two, even the lap I did alone was a bit of a weird feeling. Overall with the penalty today I had to be a good teammate and I had to help as much as I could. I think I did a good job with that and happy it worked out.”

Here’s Oscar Piastri, asked if a pole had been possible: “I don’t think so, no. I think the first lap felt good and I tried to see if anyone wanted to go in front out of the pit lane but no one did and I knew it was always going to be difficult and misjudged the braking a little bit and locked up. That was the session but good to have a decent result, it has been a while. I’ll take it.”

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen said to Sky Sports that they were aiming high: “Pierre is a class act, as you say, if you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. We haven’t always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have he has delivered. Particularly earlier in the season so to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful.

“We mustn’t forget Franco either, he’s done a great job today. I really feel we have given them a good car, and who knows? Anything is possible tomorrow.”

Here’s what he said immediately after the session: “Massive congrats to Pierre because that’s an incredible performance. We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought ‘well I think I’ll beat you in qualifying’ and here we are - he’s ahead of me again! I was disappointed not to get pole. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap. But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1. Happy to see them get a good result.”

Gasly’s advantage, it appears, seems to be over Russell’s car understeering and lacking grip in turbulent air.

P1 ☝️#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/U0hebWsjWY

He says: “It was amazing, thank you everyone. It was an incredible qualy. I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip away in evert session. I’m so happy, it’s been nine years trying to get a pole. First win [was] in Monza, to get pole is very special.”

He then pays credit to his team and the fans in Italian, and I am leaning on my Latin to get the gist of it.

“I was disappointed not to get the pole,” admits Russell who said he had been playing chess with Gasly before the game and the Frenchman won that, with Russell confident he was going to beat him in qualifying.

Alpine been in the news all weekend. Fair to say that pole lap from Gasly is better PR for the team than Flavio Briatore’s bizarre outburst in the FIA press conference yesterday. Well done that man.

His tone is evidently disappointed. In truth, given Hamilton is fifth, he is in a strong position to have the best of the weekend.

Gasly, yes, was fastest, but Russell has been the most consistent.

Piastri could be in trouble, too, for impeding earlier in the day’s sesion. Ferrari, in fourth and fifth, do not look entirely competitive.

Russell is second, Piastri third, Leclerc fourth, Hamilton fifth, Verstappen sixth, Antonelli seventh, Colapinto eighth, Norris ninth and Lindblad 10th.

He starts his flying lap, and locks up at turn 1 and exceeds track limits. That means Norris will be unable to get a tow from him too.

After being the quickest at FP2 and FP3, he is top of the pack once more with a bit over five minutes left.

Antonelli has done him a favour there, but Russell may need to return the favour in similar circumstances down the line.

Hamilton is now down in ninth, and struggling, about 0.8s off the pace.

Hamilton needs to catch Leclerc to get a tow. It failed to happen last time out.

Piastri finished Q2 in P2 but it looks likely he'll be penalised for this incident involving Lawson#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/RGzzEeqyql

Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz, Ocon, Bearman and Bortoleto are all out.

Hamilton is 10th, one-thousandth of a second quick enough to scrape through, and Leclrec ninth.

“**** me” exclaims Hamilton, without saying, ‘Asterisk’ once.

Antonelli asks for the chance to go out with another team ahead so he can get a tow of his own.

Norris now second quickest, so perhaps those brakes are up to speed.

There is some suggestion that Hamilton might need a front wing change.

The Silver Arrows working in tandem Kimi in front, George slipstreaming behind #F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/H476E91GJs

But Gasly is going fastest in his out lap.

Verstappen now goes fastest. Lawson is in behind, with Carlos Sainz making a surprise appearance up top.

Hamilton and Russell are yet to lay down times.

Norris is uncomfortable with his brakes at Monza.

Given he’s well outside of the fastest for now, the pressure is on him to make Q3.

The two Aston Martins are out, along with Yuki Tsunoda, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez.

Q2 awaits, with Gasly fastest - aiming for what would be his first pole.

Alonso, meanwhile, has wirthdrawn from the session. Things going wrong for the veteran, who must have no other hobbies.

FOUR MINUTES TO GO IN Q1TOP 6 ⬆️Gasly VerstappenColapintoAntonelliRussellHamiltonBOTTOM 6 ⬇️Hulkenberg AlbonBottasAlonsoStrollPerez#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BYdYjrjtnu

Pierre Gasly takes his Alpine for a spin. He is now fastest, with Verstappen second, and Colapinto bookending the Dutchman.

Antonelli and then Russell next, with the stricken Antonelli likely to give his colleague a tow.

The Red Bull man is 0.216s clear of Hamilton, with Piastri just behind.

No surprising stragglers just yet, but 11 minutes to go of this section.

We’ve 16 minutes left, and some cars are finally coming out to do battle.

18 minutes ahead before the final two rounds. Nobody is doing anything. As they say in football: tactically fascinating.

Monza paddock is absolutely sweltering. 33.8C out here. I just passed Fabio Capello on my way back to the media centre. He was speaking to Sky Sports Italia so I wasn’t able to give him my thoughts on where he went wrong at the 2010 World Cup.

Decent ding dong between Hamilton and Verstappen in practice earlier. Hopefully Hamilton is fired up for this. With Antonelli taking his grid drop at his home race, there’s a big opportunity for both Hamilton and Russell to close the gap this weekend.

The tifosi are ready 🙌It's time for qualifying at the Temple of Speed 👊#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/jeiTcb8Ij2

The cars will soon be out on the track, and we’ll have reports of their progress.

There are actually times when affection for a car company makes sense, despite what I said earlier.

Sound on... listen to the reception for Charles and Lewis ❤️#F1 #ItalianGP @ScuderiaFerrari pic.twitter.com/kk6BvA1UdC

As touched on earlier, Lewis Hamilton has to hope Charles Leclerc will work with him.

The Monegasque (look it up) is the junior partner at this point, whether he wants to be or not. That might not make him entirely delighted, but he can tow the British driver around and give him a launch for fast laps, if he’s feeling helpful.

Everyone now has access to PowerPoint, which means we all now have to have, “learnings.”

Imagine if someone you met in real life said that to you.

3 hours of laps and learnings done.#ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/GTvOvL5L5M

Given Antonelli is still one of the quickest on the track, it would be no surprise if he can at least make the top 10.

Favourable accidents and yellow flags might offer up more opportunities, too, but both Hamilton and Russell need to strike while they have such a clear advantage.

George Russell tops Lewis Hamilton in final practice in Monza 🇮🇹💪 pic.twitter.com/jxIO13aRX6

I’m as big a fan of F1 as the next man, assuming the next man quite likes F1, but there is something strange about supporting a car company, isn’t there?

🇮🇹 Sentendo il calore dell'Italia! 🥰🇬🇧 Feeling the warmth of Italy! 🥰 pic.twitter.com/ze6Ww1Z0zx

The session starts in around 40 minutes, so drivers are on their Gameboys and Instagram, and reading the weekend edition of The Telegraph.

Words we live by, this weekend and always ❤️ pic.twitter.com/0QoGlpzOHI

Here’s our interview with Alex Albon about a grim weekend at Monza.

“Alex Albon remembers the 2022 Italian Grand Prix well. He had been looking forward to it. ‘We had a car which was good down the straights that year so I was quite excited to be going to Monza,” the Williams driver recalls, a little wistfully.

‘We did FP1 and FP2 and sure enough we were quick so I was like: ‘This is going to be a good weekend.’

“Albon could not have been more wrong. He remembers waking at around 1am that night and being unable to get back to sleep.

“What happened next was the stuff of nightmares. Albon called the doctor, was diagnosed with appendicitis, sent to San Gerardo Hospital in Monza for surgery, only to suffer an unexpected complication during the procedure, which resulted in acute respiratory failure.”

He shares the joint record with Michael Schumacher for most wins at Monza.

Schumacher, a Ferrari legend, ended his career with five. Hamilton has the same.

Sport loves an emotional link to records, so be prepared for this to become a big moment.

Five wins apiece for Michael and Lewis 🖐#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/j10lMygYft

The Italian team are bringing an upgrade engine to Monza for the weekend.

Hamilton would desperately love to go out at the top after what is a remarkable return to decent form after some years of desperate struggle.

With Antonelli possibly out of the running this weekend, this is the chance to change the - *spits in self-scorn* - narrative.

Russell might have incurred a penalty if he had done this in qualifying.

The Mercedes man blocked Oscar Piastri’s run at a corner, forcing some heavy braking from his rival.

Thankfully, Piastri ducked out, and thankfully for Russell, he’s not facing censure.

A near miss for Oscar Piastri! 😬 pic.twitter.com/y6UMu8wIDM

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton go racing! 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Zs8u8h4XoT

The former world champion is still looking for more from his car.

“Just looking at the deltas there, I was losing something like 0.6secs to George on the straights, which is something we need to look into,” Hamilton said yesterday, before explaining his conundrum for qualifying, suggesting he may go out after Leclerc.

“The tow is everything here so [I’m] likely to be looking for the tow.”

Because Antonelli exceeded the limit of parts used for his engine, he is taking a grid penalty at Monza.

Few would entirely rule out a storming ride for him on Sunday to end up top of the pack, but is is clearly a huge task for him to score points of any kind with that disadvantage.

They are now likely both past their peaks, but Hamilton and Verstappen recalled their battles of 2021 when they clashed in practice earlier.

Verstappen was already hacked off with Hamilton for seemingly obstructing his path earlier in the session, and they almost came together in the dying moments of the session.

Hamilton needed to take the escape road at the first chicane, where the pair made contact in 2021, as Verstappen looked to slip around his occasional rival. The two of them scarcely avoided another contact.

On the radios, Verstappen claimed, “He caused that,” while Hamilton reported to Ferrari that he was, “Blocked by Max.” Perhaps there will be more aggro later.

The full list of times from earlier today.

FP3 CLASSIFICATIONRussell in the box seat heading into qualifying#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BUrCsv92dT

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

#2014. Manchester United’s 34-goal defensive record shows scale of Pochettino’s task

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Manchester United have conceded more goals than any other club in Europe’s five major domestic leagues this season, underlining the scale of the challenge facing Mauricio Pochettino following Sunday’s 4-0 defeat at Liverpool.

Pochettino’s first match in charge ended in a heavy defeat at Anfield after defender Leny Yoro was sent off in the eighth minute. Although the dismissal left United facing an uphill struggle, their defensive record suggests the new head coach has inherited problems that extend well beyond one match.

According to an analysis published by the Premier League, United have conceded 34 goals in 16 matches across all competitions this season. That is the highest total of any club in Europe’s five major domestic leagues, with Sunday’s defeat adding four more goals to an already concerning record.

The Premier League also calculated Liverpool’s expected goals at 4.38, suggesting the hosts created enough chances to have won by an even greater margin. United’s difficulties began when Matthijs de Ligt misjudged a long ball, and Yoro fouled Alexander Isak as the Liverpool forward attempted to break through on goal.

Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the resulting free-kick, with Florian Wirtz doubling Liverpool’s advantage just three minutes later. Rio Ngumoha and substitute Victor Munoz completed the scoring after half-time.

The defeat left United 19th in the Premier League, with just eight points from their opening 11 matches and one league victory all season. Pochettino acknowledged the painful nature of the result but argued that the early dismissal had transformed the contest. He also questioned whether Yoro should have been sent off, given the circumstances of the challenge on Isak.

The Argentine’s first tactical plan was disrupted almost immediately, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how United might perform under him with a full complement of players.

Nevertheless, the defensive record accumulated before his arrival makes clear that improving the team’s organisation will be a central part of his work. The Premier League’s analysis highlighted De Ligt’s mistake before the sending-off and the opportunities Liverpool continued to create against United’s depleted defence.

United return to Champions League action on Wednesday when they travel to Portugal to face Sporting, giving Pochettino little time to address the issues exposed at Anfield. The fixture offers an early opportunity to assess how he intends to organise his defence and whether the team can respond to another damaging result.

Pochettino must also decide how to balance defensive stability with the need to improve results. United’s league position means they cannot afford to spend too long finding that balance. The circumstances of Sunday’s defeat were unusual, and the red card undoubtedly made United’s task more difficult. But conceding 34 goals in 16 matches points to a wider problem that will require sustained improvement rather than a reaction to one result.

For Pochettino, making United harder to beat is an obvious starting point. Wednesday’s trip to Sporting will provide his next opportunity to begin that process.

#2013. Ex-Liverpool and Wolves star enters Blackpool FC managerial frame

Former Premier League and England international defender, Conor Coady, has reportedly emerged as a leading contender to replace Ian Evatt at League One strugglers, Blackpool.

That is according to an update from Pete O'Rourke via X, with the Tangerines beginning third-tier life without their former defender with one point from a possible six.

A 2-1 loss to Lancashire rivals, Wigan Athletic, at Bloomfield Road on Saturday lunchtime was followed up by an encouraging draw against Russell Martin's in-form Leicester City on Tuesday night, with Niall Ennis equalising Will Alves' opener.

Blackpool are currently 20th in League One having taken just 13 points from 15 matches, and whilst the club still have a game in hand to play over many divisional rivals, only a two-goal swing separates them and Doncaster Rovers, who occupy the final relegation place.

Blackpool have endured mixed fortunes since their relegation from the Championship three-and-a-half years ago, with whoever replaces Evatt being the fifth head coach at Bloomfield Road since then.

Evatt was able to guide the Seasiders to a 13th-placed finish last season, ending the campaign with four wins on the bounce, but departed the club last week on his 45th birthday, and attention has now turned as to who will be his successor in the long run.

Steve Thompson led the fixtures against Wigan and Leicester, but as per O'Rourke, it has been claimed that Coady, 33, has emerged as a 'top contender' for the role, just weeks after confirming his retirement from playing.

The centre-back amassed over 300 combined appearances at Premier League and Championship level, and is best known for his spells at Liverpool, Wolves, Everton and Wrexham, which included a second-tier title win at Molineux, as well as earning 10 England caps.

It is stated that the England Under-21s assistant has already impressed higher-ups at the Football Association after landing said role two months' ago.

FLW have looked at the top 12 EFL League One clubs and have ranked them smallest to largest based on their average home attendance in the 26/27 season

Coady terminated his Wrexham contract in August after making just six appearances under Phil Parkinson at the Racecourse Ground, and immediately turned his focus to coaching.

Indeed, he was offered a role within Liverpool's academy setup, working alongside former Blackpool midfielder, Jay Spearing, before replacing Ashley Cole as part of Lee Carsley's setup with the Young Lions, who have recently won successive UEFA Under-21 European Championships.

It remains to be seen if Coady does land his first full-time managerial role on the Fylde Coast, but when asked about what the future holds, he recently said: "I'm not massively in a rush because I want to make sure it's (the decision is) right."

There has, unsurprisingly, been plenty of discourse as to who the Blackpool hierarchy will turn to next in an attempt to improve the club's fortunes.

Coady, of course, would be a high-profile name based off his playing exploits, but the St Helens native isn't the only figure linked with the job.

Tangerines fans, who would you like to see named as Ian Evatt's successor? Comment below!

Indeed, it was previously reported by O'Rourke that former Pool centre-back, Matt Lawlor, has been shortlisted, with the 38-year-old currently boasting a 37% win ratio at local rivals and League Two outfit, Fleetwood Town.

Lawlor became the Cod Army's permanent head coach in March, and whilst league form has remained inconsistent, his EFL Cup exploits have gained plenty of notoriety, especially after a historic penalty shootout triumph over Premier League champions, Arsenal, on October 27th, which set up a quarter-final date with Everton next month.

#2012. Roy Keane questions Manchester United standards after Liverpool humiliation

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Former Manchester United captain Roy Keane has criticised the players’ performance and questioned supporters applauding them after Sunday’s 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, insisting the early red card was no excuse for the manner of the loss.

Mauricio Pochettino’s first match in charge unravelled when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes at Anfield. Liverpool scored twice inside 13 minutes and added two more goals after the break, leaving United 19th in the Premier League.

Speaking on Sky Sports, Keane challenged the suggestion that United’s performance was understandable because they had played most of the match with 10 men.

“Fans are applauding. Applauding what?” he asked, before describing the performance as “rubbish”.

Keane argued that United should have shown greater fight and quality, claiming Liverpool could have scored eight or nine goals. He also questioned why responsibility for the club’s problems so often fell on managers, owners and executives rather than the players themselves.

Some travelling supporters applauded the team after the final whistle, potentially recognising the difficulty of playing more than 80 minutes with a numerical disadvantage. Keane, however, viewed the reaction as evidence of declining expectations.

Keane also challenged fellow former United captain Gary Neville, who had suggested the early dismissal made the result more understandable. Neville was far from satisfied with United’s performance, though, and separately accused the club’s hierarchy of negligence for failing to strengthen the defence.

The disagreement reflected two concerns surrounding United: the players’ response to adversity and the quality of the squad available to Pochettino. Liverpool’s goals came from Dominik Szoboszlai, Florian Wirtz, Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz, with the hosts creating numerous further opportunities.

Pochettino defended his players’ commitment afterwards and questioned Yoro’s dismissal, arguing that Alexander Isak had not established control of the ball when the defender challenged him. United have taken just eight points from 11 Premier League matches, leaving their new manager with little time to improve results. They travel to Sporting in the Champions League on Wednesday before returning to domestic action.

Keane’s criticism adds to the scrutiny surrounding the squad following another heavy defeat to their fiercest rivals. For Pochettino, the immediate challenge is to improve defensive organisation while restoring confidence in a side struggling near the bottom of the table.

#2011. Manchester United to appeal Leny Yoro red card as Fernandes questions officials

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Manchester United have notified the Football Association of their intention to appeal against Leny Yoro’s red card during Sunday’s 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, with captain Bruno Fernandes among those questioning the decision.

The French defender was dismissed in the eighth minute at Anfield after bringing down Alexander Isak outside the penalty area. Referee Sam Barrott ruled that Yoro had denied an obvious goalscoring opportunity, with Dominik Szoboszlai scoring from the resulting free-kick.

According to Sky Sports, United intend to challenge the decision, with Isak’s chances of regaining possession central to the dispute. Mauricio Pochettino questioned whether Isak would have reached the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens, a view shared by midfielder Kobbie Mainoo.

Fernandes told the BBC after the match that it was “never a red card”.

“To make a mistake like this can change a game,” he said, as reported by the Press Association. The Portuguese midfielder nevertheless accepted that United were responsible for conceding from the subsequent free-kick.

Former Premier League referee Dermot Gallagher offered a different assessment on Sky Sports’ Ref Watch programme, supporting Barrott’s decision while acknowledging the uncertainty over whether Isak would have reached the ball before Lammens.

“I think most people would have expected a red card,” Gallagher said.

An attacker’s likelihood of retaining or regaining possession is among the factors referees must consider when assessing whether a foul has denied an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

United host Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday in Pochettino’s first home match in charge. Unless the appeal succeeds, Yoro will serve a one-match suspension against the Bees. United sit 19th in the Premier League, having won just one of their opening 11 matches. Yoro remains eligible for Wednesday’s Champions League fixture against Sporting, before attention turns to a crucial domestic fixture for Pochettino’s side.

#2010. Ashley Barnes reacts to huge moment for ex-Burnley star Maxime Esteve

Maxime Esteve made his Champions League debut for RB Leipzig against Lens on Tuesday night, and one of his former teammates was cheering him on.

One of the biggest costs that comes with relegation from the Premier League can be the loss of players that comes with it. Even relegated sides have some players who will be wanted elsewhere, and many will have clauses in their contracts entitling them to leave in the event that their teams go down by the end of a season.

This exodus took place at the end of the 2025-26 season for Burnley, just as it routinely does for clubs relegated from this level, and in the case of defender Maxime Esteve the offer was an appealing one. The 24-year-old centre-back signed for RB Leipzig in the summer, and although he's primarily been used as a squad player by the Bundesliga outfit through the opening weeks of this season, he was included in their team for their Champions League match against RC Lens on Tuesday night, his debut in the competition.

It turned out to be a successful night for both the player and his new club. RB Leipzig won the match 3-1, and Esteve scored strongly for his performance before being withdrawn midway through the second half with cramp. And after the match, when he posted to social media about his delight at making his Champions League debut, one of his former Burnley teammates was there in the replies with a show of support for him.

Posting to the social media platform Instagram after RB Leipzig's 3-1 win over RC Lens in the Champions League on Tuesday night, Maxime Esteve couldn't contain his delight at having made his first appearance in Europe's premier club competition, saying, "First Champions League game, at home, and a win to go with it."

Esteve was clearly very pleased to have been given the opportunity in such a prestigious tournament: "A night I won’t forget. Thanks to the team and to our fans for the atmosphere. Let’s keep going."

Would you have wanted Burnley to keep hold of Maxime Esteve for 2026-27? Let us know in the comments below!

Among those congratulating Esteve in the comments was one of his former teammates. Ashley Barnes has played over 300 games for Burnley, but his first spell ended before Esteve arrived at the club. But the former Brighton and Norwich striker returned to the Lancashire club in January 2025 and extended his contract for a year at the end of the 2024-25 season, meaning that the two were in the same Clarets squad for a season and a half.

And it's clear from the reactions to this post - not only from Barnes - but also from a number of Burnley fans, that the central defender is still thought of fondly at Turf Moor, almost half a season on from his departure from their club.

Maxime Esteve has been tipped for the top after excelling for the Clarets this season

Maxime Esteve's move to RB Leipzig hasn't gone completely according to plan for the 24-year-old defender. He has only made five appearances for his new club since arriving in the summer, of which three have been starts. But an assured performance will only have strengthened his case for a more regular berth in their starting eleven.

This is an exciting time to be at the club. RB Leipzig are in fourth place in the Bundesliga, and although Bayern Munich remain the clear favourites to win the league title, Leipzig are only three points behind current leaders Borussia Dortmund.

It's all a long way removed from Burnley's dismal 2025-26 Premier League season, which ended with the Clarets relegated in 19th place having picked up just 22 points all season, leaving them 19 points short of safety.

Ashley Barnes, meanwhile, stayed at Turf Moor following relegation after agreeing another contract extension with Burnley during the summer. But Barnes has not been a central part of the Burnley team since his 2025 return to Turf Moor. He only made seven appearances for them in the Premier League last season, all of which came from the bench and which amounted to just 41 minutes of game time.

This season has seen Barnes get even less game time for Burnley. He has yet to make an appearance for them in the Championship in 2026-27, although at 37 years of age, the striker may be preparing for a post-playing career in coaching rather than being fully focussed on playing. It's already been reported that he'll be joining the club's coaching staff at the end of this season.

The only sighting of him that Burnley fans have had on the pitch this season came with a 45-minute cameo appearance in a Premier League 2 fixture against West Ham United towards the end of October. But the fact that he should be giving such support to one of his former teammates is a positive sign for what Burnley fans can expect from him as a coach.

#2009. Pochettino identifies January transfer priority as Manchester United’s goals dry up

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino reportedly wants to sign a striker in the January transfer window, with Benjamin Sesko not expected to return from injury until the new year at the earliest.

The Argentine’s first match in charge ended in a 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday, leaving United 19th in the Premier League with just one victory from their opening 11 matches. While defensive shortcomings attracted much of the criticism following the defeat at Anfield, strengthening United’s attack appears to be a priority for the new head coach.

According to The Times, United’s hierarchy and Pochettino agree that the squad requires strengthening in January, despite the club’s preference for conducting major transfer business during the summer. Sesko’s prolonged absence has limited United’s attacking options, while Joshua Zirkzee has scored just 11 goals in 86 appearances since joining from Bologna’s Serie A rivals Fiorentina in 2024.

Monaco striker Folarin Balogun has been identified as a potential target. The United States international worked under Pochettino at international level and has expressed a desire to leave the French club.

Writing in The Independent, Miguel Delaney suggests United could have scope to spend £150m in January, although such expenditure would affect the club’s longer-term recruitment plans. That figure does not represent a confirmed transfer budget, and United have yet to announce any agreement to sign a new striker.

Pochettino’s immediate challenge is finding a solution with his existing squad. United face Sporting in the Champions League on Wednesday before returning to domestic action against Brentford.

With more than a month before the transfer window opens, the Argentine has little choice but to find a way of improving United’s attacking output with the players already at his disposal.

#2008. Chelsea Monitor Jarrod Bowen And Crysencio Summerville

Chelsea’s wide-player search has moved back into focus after the Guardian reported that the club are monitoring West Ham pair Jarrod Bowen and Crysencio Summerville.

The update lands during a busy early market for Xabi Alonso’s incoming rebuild.

The Guardian’s latest transfer round-up states that Chelsea like both West Ham forwards, while an earlier report noted Chelsea and Manchester United had tracked Summerville.

That same earlier update also said Aston Villa, Chelsea and Everton had expressed interest in Bowen.

West Ham pulling away at Stamford Bridge 👀Jarrod Bowen stuns Chelsea early before Crysencio Summerville doubles the lead. pic.twitter.com/Ktwr4pKZGH

Alonso officially begins work on July 1, with Chelsea confirming he has signed a four-year contract to lead the men’s team.

The winger search is not just about adding more attacking names. It is about identifying profiles who can quickly give Chelsea sharper final-third decisions.

Bowen would offer immediate Premier League output, penalty-box timing and a direct threat from the right.

Summerville, meanwhile, fits the younger, explosive one-v-one profile that would sit neatly inside Alonso’s longer-term wing plan.

Read Chelsea has already tracked the separate Summerville angle, but this latest dual link sharpens the picture.

Chelsea appear to be testing two different solutions to the same problem: proven reliability or higher-upside acceleration.

With pre-season closing in, that is exactly the sort of market check Alonso needs before deciding how much of Chelsea’s attacking rebuild should lean on speed, touchline width and more ruthless wide output.

#2007. John Eustace to be sacked at Derby County? Journalist drops fresh update

Derby County's 3-0 defeat to Wolverhampton Wanderers at Molineux has only increased the speculation over John Eustace's future at Pride Park.

The Rams started off the encounter in encouraging fashion, but, ultimately, could not convert one of their early chances past the experienced Jose Sa.

Eustace's side had returned from the year's final international break with a 2-0 defeat to promotion-chasing Southampton at St. Mary's, and a fourth away defeat in five was confirmed as Cesar Peixoto's outfit turned up the heat with a brace from Adam Armstrong and a merited goal from highly-rated winger, Mateus Mane.

The heavy loss in the West Midlands, coupled with Preston North End's surprise 4-0 rout over Cardiff City in South Wales means that Derby will kickstart the Championship's 17th matchweek at the foot of the table - a far cry from what many predicted was in store for Eustace's side in pre-season.

The experienced head coach has been under pressure for some time, and now scrutiny over his position has reappeared ahead of a must-win encounter against his former club, Watford, on Saturday.

Just last month, Eustace revealed that he retained the full backing of Derby owner, David Clowes, over the potential to turn the club's fortunes around.

Since then, the Rams have accumulated four points from a possible 18, with a sole victory coming through a 3-1 success over Bolton Wanderers on November 6th.

Speaking to local radio post-match, Eustace reaffirmed the confidence he has in himself and his squad to get out of the current situation, but no word has come from the club since the full-time whistle at Molineux, which only increased speculation.

However, BBC Derby Sport's Dominic Dietrich has since confirmed that, as things stand, Eustace will lead the team for Saturday's clash against the Hornets, who, earlier on Wednesday, confirmed Edward Iordanescu as Alessio Dionisi's successor.

For the second time in three seasons, Derby are staring at the prospect of a Championship relegation battle.

Eustace has now lost 36 of his 81 matches in charge, equating in a win ratio of just 36%, and, unsurprisingly, the fresh update has caused a stir.

One fan commented: "This is quite disrespectful to the fanbase now. Actually not now. But a few games ago. Two possible reasons both really bad. Financial reasons: I can't believe this. Because relegation will be much more expensive. Blind loyalty: Even worse than financial mismanagement."

"It’s an insult to the fans that there is no official communication from the club," was another response from a displeased Rams follower.

"Simply kicking the can down the road. Irrespective of any result against Watford, it’ll just be papering over the canyon. Fundamental change is needed," stated another supporter.

Echoing such sentiments, one comment read: "Was only last season the chants of 'Eustace barmy army' were loud and proud. Football is a very fickle game. Clowes holding his nerve. Saturday is going to be interesting...."

Rams fans, how much longer can David Clowes afford to stick with John Eustace? Comment below!

Another supporter claimed: "I could understand him keeping his job if we’re losing games by fine margins and they players were all trying but we’ve been utter crap. Wolves had near on 40 shots last night. And his post-match interviews are insane! There is definitely something going on behind the scenes."

"How much worse does it need to get? How much worse can it get? 10 points from 51 in this awful league is a disaster," debated another frustrated fan.

Derby are now five points adrift of safety with 29 matches remaining, and whilst that allows plenty of time for the club's fortunes to change, there have been little signs that such feats will occur under Eustace.

The former Birmingham City and Blackburn Rovers boss does have experience of staving off relegation, but, no doubt some of the frustration felt by supporters stems from the actions taken at their relegation rivals.

Derby County chairman David Clowes is coming under fire from some fans - but is it too harsh?

Preston have taken seven points from their last three matches under Graham Alexander after he replaced Paul Heckingbottom, whilst Burnley, Watford and now Lincoln City have already opted to make managerial changes.

The Rams have won just five league matches since the start of April, and whilst injuries to key men such as Patrick Agyemang haven't helped Eustace, such circumstances were not expected whatsoever.

#2004. What can Mauricio Pochettino spend on January targets at Manchester United?

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United spent heavily during the summer, bringing Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba to Old Trafford for a combined £148million.

Despite the summer transfers, Michael Carrick failed to keep his job and was replaced by Mauricio Pochettino.

With United struggling, Pochettino is expected to bring a few new names in the January transfer window. The manager is reportedly expected to bring in no more than two players, with a new striker understood to be his biggest priority.

With the summer investment, the club is left with less flexibility as Pochettino looks to address several weaknesses in his squad.

Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino could have less than £50million to spend in January, leaving the Argentine with limited room to spend during the winter transfer window.

According to reports from the Daily Mail, United are working within financial restrictions and are unlikely to sanction any major spending in January. The club are also mindful of the Premier League’s financial regulations, which could make it difficult to fund major names.

Benjamin Sesko’s injury problems and Joshua Zirkzee’s disappointing form have increased the need for another centre-forward.

Monaco striker Folarin Balogun is among the names linked with United. Pochettino already knows the United States international from their time together with the national team, which could make him an interesting option.

Leeds United’s Dominic Calvert-Lewin and former Brentford striker Ivan Toney, currently playing for Al-Ahli, have also been mentioned as targets.

A left-back is another position United want to address. The club failed to bring in proper competition for Luke Shaw during the summer, despite being linked with Barcelona’s Alejandro Balde and Rayan Ait-Nouri.

However, the budget means Pochettino may have to choose his priorities carefully rather than address every problem in one window.

United recorded revenue of £677.6million despite not playing European football last season. However, the Premier League’s Squad Cost Ratio rules restrict spending on player and head coach wages, transfer repayments and agent fees to 85 per cent of football revenue, plus net profit from player sales.

January could become a window of careful decisions for United and Pochettino but looking at their current position and form, they need far more than just 50 million. In this budget, Pochettino needs to be careful who he brings in to improve their standings.

#2003. Chelsea World Cup Knockout Load Gives Xabi Alonso Pre-Season Problem

Chelsea’s World Cup contingent has moved from a group-stage watchlist into a genuine Xabi Alonso planning problem.

Chelsea’s own tournament update confirms that Enzo Fernandez, Mike Penders, Moises Caicedo, Kendry Paez, Malo Gusto and Jorrel Hato have reached the Round of 32.

England have also progressed after their final Group L win over Panama, which keeps Reece James and Trevoh Chalobah inside the wider knockout picture.

For supporters, that is a status marker. For Alonso, it is where summer pride starts to become pre-season compression.

The concern is not simply volume. It is where the minutes are landing.

Enzo has not missed a minute for Argentina, while Caicedo has remained central for Ecuador and captained them in the 2-1 win over Germany.

Those are not fringe workloads. They are the two midfield profiles Chelsea have built large parts of their control game around.

Alonso’s first Chelsea pre-season was always going to demand clarity through the middle of the pitch.

Instead, the players most central to that reset are still operating in knockout football.

Caicedo’s Ecuador role is the cleanest example. Read Chelsea has already assessed how his captaincy display against Germany strengthened his leadership case, but the next layer is more complicated.

Every additional knockout tie gives him more tournament rhythm, more authority and more fatigue.

Argentina’s route against Cape Verde keeps him on a glamorous stage at exactly the moment Chelsea need to settle his role, mood and tactical responsibilities under Alonso.

If Madrid-related noise continues around him, the club cannot afford a sluggish July handover.

Reece James started England’s first two matches before a hamstring issue ruled him out of the Panama game, according to the Guardian.

England still topped the group and moved into a last-32 tie with DR Congo, but James’ situation is exactly the kind of detail Chelsea’s medical team will monitor closely.

Chelsea have already had to plan around a large World Cup group.

The broader issue was clear in Read Chelsea’s earlier pre-season workload piece, but the knockout stage sharpens it because the returns will now be staggered.

Enzo brings a maximum group-stage load. Caicedo brings captaincy responsibility and heavy Ecuador minutes.

James brings knockout qualification mixed with another hamstring-management question.

Gusto and Hato remain tied to France and the Netherlands, while Penders and Paez are still absorbing tournament environments before club reintegration.

That is a spine issue, not a fringe issue.

Alonso needs automatisms in possession, spacing around the double pivot, clearer full-back behaviour and pressing triggers from midfield.

Those details do not bed in properly when key players arrive in drips after a major summer tournament.

Players returning from knockout football can bring competitive sharpness that closed-door friendlies cannot replicate.

Caicedo captaining Ecuador through pressure games matters. Enzo playing high-leverage minutes for Argentina matters.

Gusto and Hato absorbing tournament detail also helps Chelsea’s defensive reset.

But Chelsea cannot treat every tournament minute as clean preparation.

Alonso must decide who returns straight into tactical work, who needs a genuine pause and who can handle August without creating an avoidable injury bill by September.

That is where the James situation feels central.

If Chelsea’s captain carries a World Cup hamstring warning, the club’s right-sided structure becomes more than a selection debate.

It becomes an availability question that touches Gusto, the wider defensive rebuild and the need for control from midfield.

Read Chelsea has already looked at James’ captaincy test under Alonso, and the injury layer now makes that test sharper.

This is the hidden cost of a strong international footprint.

Chelsea want players good enough to survive deep into tournaments.

Alonso now has to make sure that status does not leave his first league weeks short of the very control those players are meant to provide.

Bolton Wanderers have had a positive return to the Championship, as they look to establish themselves back at this level.

Steven Schumacher has done a fantastic job with the Trotters since his appointment, and whilst he will be pleased at how they’ve coped this season, they are struggling for consistency.

Therefore, there is plenty of room to improve, and the Bolton boss will know that the cushion to the bottom three can be eaten into very quickly if they don’t keep picking up results.

So, January could be crucial, and one player who is likely to be on the market is Jeremy Monga.

The winger joined Man City from Leicester for around £10m in the summer, and he was immediately loaned to Swansea, which seemed like a good fit for the player.

However, with Moussa Yeo, Elijah Just and Joseph Opoku also joining the Welsh club in the summer, it’s fair to say competition for places is fierce in the final third.

The past few months will be hugely frustrating for Monga, and video footage of the player wandering around the pitch on his own after the recent game against West Brom left many feeling sorry for the 17-year-old, who has seen his career stall.

As a result, it’s fair to say that Monga and his parent club will be counting down the days until the January window opens, so his season-long loan can be cut short.

FLW have ranked the 10 best players in the EFL Championship for the 2026/27 season aged 22 or below, including a pair of Middlesbrough stars.

Of course, Vitor Matos’ departure from Swansea could change things, but the Welsh club are stacked for talent in the final third.

Elijah Just, Moussa Yeo and Joseph Opoku were among the summer additions, so game time was always going to be difficult to come by for Monga, and it’s hard to envisage him forcing his way into the XI even under a new head coach.

Following on from that, if City do send Monga somewhere else, they will be prioritising first-team football for the player, which could make Bolton the perfect fit.

Right now, the likes of Thierry Gale, Samuel Iling-Junior and Kylian Dong have all struggled for form, even if Gale has made some decent contributions earlier on in the campaign.

Nevertheless, attacking reinforcements will be the priority, and Monga could flourish in Schumacher’s setup.

Unlike many newly-promoted teams, Bolton are a front-footed, attacking team, and they haven’t been scared of taking the game to their opponents - as the likes of West Ham and Wolves found out, even if they did ultimately lose against the Hammers.

As part of his XI, Schumacher wants wingers who can hug the touchline, and he gives them freedom to carry the ball and express themselves.

That’s exactly what Monga needs right now, and, despite his age, the England youth international proved on occasions with Leicester last season that he can cause problems at this level.

We know that Bolton don’t have the biggest budget in the Championship, so they have to be smart in their recruitment, and they have made some good signings in the past few windows.

But, January is also difficult, and you don’t want to get sucked into paying over the odds for players, so it’s all about finding the balance.

In Monga, Bolton could get an exciting talent on loan, and, if it does work out, it will only enhance their reputation for developing players, which could be crucial moving forward.

So, it’s certainly one that they should pursue, and January will be a massive month for the Trotters if they want to ensure they can have a comfortable end to the campaign.

#2001. Too late, FA overturns Leny Yoro’s Liverpool red card in Pochettino’s first game

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United have received a major boost ahead of their Premier League meeting with Brentford after the Football Association overturned Leny Yoro’s red card against Liverpool.

The defender was sent off just eight minutes into Sunday’s 4-0 defeat at Anfield after bringing down Alexander Isak during a challenge that referee Sam Barrott judged to be a denial of a clear goalscoring opportunity.

However, Manchester United decided to contest the decision, and their appeal has now been successful. The FA confirmed that Yoro’s one-match suspension has been removed following a successful claim of wrongful dismissal.

“The Manchester United player was sent off for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity during their Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday 22 November. The independent Regulatory Commission’s written reasons for its decision will be published in due course,” the FA’s official statement read.

The decision means the French defender is available for Saturday’s meeting with Brentford at Old Trafford, giving Mauricio Pochettino another option in defence.

Mauricio Pochettino was furious with the original decision, particularly because it came so early in the game and left United playing with ten men for almost the entire match.

The United manager believed Isak’s heavy touch had taken the ball away from the Liverpool forward and put Senne Lammens in a position to collect it.

Speaking after the defeat, Pochettino questioned whether Yoro had actually committed a foul and insisted the defender had no intention of bringing Isak down.

“The ball wasn’t in his control,” Pochettino said.

“Isak, when he saw the control wasn’t good, it’s normal to delay, and stop to the run. In that moment that Yoro came from the back, and you go down.”

The Argentine also made his feelings clear about the nature of the contact.

“But all that we play football; you know that wasn’t intentional. That is never a foul,” he added.

The FA’s decision will come as a relief to Manchester United but perhaps too late. United suffered a heavy 4-0 defeat at Anfield after Yoro’s red. Pochettino would have had a chance in the game if VAR had overturned the red card, but United got another decision against them in the Premier League.

Although the appeal cannot change the outcome of the heavy defeat at Anfield, it at least means Pochettino will not lose one of his defensive options because of a decision that the club successfully challenged.

#1999. Malo Gusto’s Kante Lesson Gives Chelsea A £75m Xabi Alonso Decision

Malo Gusto’s World Cup has suddenly become more than a France subplot for Chelsea. It is now a live assessment of whether Xabi Alonso inherits a right-back worth protecting, reshaping or trading at the peak of his market.

Chelsea’s own interview with Gusto this week underlined the human part of that equation. The 23-year-old spoke about learning from N’Golo Kante, calling the former Blue one of the best midfielders France have produced and stressing the value of his example on and off the pitch.

That matters because Kante is not just a nostalgic reference point. He remains the standard Chelsea supporters still use when judging humility, intensity and reliability in a high-pressure dressing room.

For Gusto, those qualities arrive at a decisive moment. Reports around the player’s future claim Chelsea value him at around £75million, with the imminent Marco Palestra deal creating a more crowded full-back picture.

That number looks aggressive, but the logic is clear. Gusto is young, capped by France, under contract, Premier League-tested and capable of playing in several defensive structures.

🚨🚨| NEW: Chelsea are open to selling Malo Gusto this summer, with his agent already in 𝐓𝐀𝐋𝐊𝐒 with Manchester City and Inter. Chelsea will only sell if their valuation is met.{@siphillipssport} pic.twitter.com/vNR2bWud9F

The easiest reading of Gusto’s Kante comments is sentimental. It should not be.

For Alonso, who officially begins work on July 1, the important detail is what those comments say about the player Chelsea have been developing.

Gusto has not always looked completely settled at Stamford Bridge. His best games have carried thrust, speed and recovery power, while his less convincing spells have raised questions about final-ball quality and defensive concentration.

That uncertainty is exactly why the next coach matters.

Alonso’s previous teams have leaned heavily on wide players who can receive under pressure, attack space early and still protect the back line when possession breaks down. Gusto has the athletic base for that job.

The test is whether his decision-making can be refined enough to make him a structural piece rather than a rotation asset.

That is where the Kante reference lands with force. Chelsea do not need Gusto to imitate Kante’s position. They need him to absorb the same professional standard: repeat actions, clean defensive choices, no wasted emotion and total commitment to the collective rhythm.

The Marco Palestra deal changes the right side of Chelsea’s squad immediately. Read Chelsea has already examined how Palestra’s arrival offers a tactical clue over Alonso’s defensive plans, and that pressure is now sharpened by market noise around Gusto.

Chelsea can frame the situation in two ways.

One is profit-led. If a club comes close to the reported £75million level, selling a player signed from Lyon for a much lower fee becomes a powerful PSR lever.

The other is football-led. If Alonso sees Gusto as a high-upside wing-back who fits his model, selling him just as the coaching environment becomes more suitable would carry long-term risk.

The complication is Reece James. The captain’s fitness issues, including his current England hamstring concern, mean Chelsea still need genuine right-sided depth.

Palestra may be part of the future, but Gusto is already part of the present. Chelsea have too often needed emergency solutions in that area to treat proven depth lightly.

That is why Read Chelsea’s recent look at James awaiting hamstring scan results matters in this debate. Right-back remains one of the most talented areas of the squad, but also one of the least straightforward.

This is why Gusto’s France rhythm is more valuable than a simple tournament diary entry. Chelsea are watching a player operate inside an elite international camp, learn from a club legend and handle a public transfer valuation that can change his status overnight.

Alonso’s first decision does not have to be final, but it does have to be clear.

If Gusto stays, he needs a defined role early in pre-season and a pathway that makes sense alongside Palestra and James. If Chelsea sell, they need to do it at a number that justifies weakening one of the few squad areas where youth, speed and top-level experience already overlap.

Gusto’s Kante lesson, then, is not just a feel-good Chelsea connection. It is a reminder of the standard Alonso must demand before deciding whether £75million is a price to accept or a warning sign that Chelsea should hold firm.

#1998. London club pushing to sign Sheffield Wednesday player - Challinor happy to offload

Sheffield Wednesday may not have taken all three points from their away clash with Stevenage on Tuesday, but a goalless draw has kept them in the promotion mix as the halfway mark of League One creeps closer.

Back-to-back wins over Plymouth Argyle and Barnsley was the perfect start league-wise for new manager Dave Challinor, and it keeps them in the mix for the top two ahead of a busy period of fixtures.

Until the January transfer window opens though, there's not much scope for Wednesday to do anything transfer-wise - they're still under the guidance of an EFL-agreed business plan and budget restriction, which didn't stop them from landing some quality players in the summer, but it did restrict how many deals they could do.

FLW have looked at the top 12 EFL League One clubs and have ranked them smallest to largest based on their average home attendance in the 26/27 season

Right now, Challinor has pretty much a big squad to choose from for his 18-man matchday selection, and it's left young defender Ernie Weaver out in the cold, despite his impressive performances for the Owls during last season's Championship struggles.

Early on in the 2025-26 season, prior to Wednesday being placed into administration by disgraced former owner Dejphon Chansiri, Henrik Pedersen gave a chance to Weaver with defensive options limited.

Having just turned 19, Weaver made his first Championship start in a 2-0 away win against Portsmouth, and at the heart of the Owls backline, they went on a three-match unbeaten run when he was starting matches.

Despite rapidly gaining plaudits, a 5-0 defeat at the hands of Coventry City in October would be his final outing of the season, as a troublesome ankle injury would cut short Weaver's campaign, which happened just before administration came into place.

Weaver has appeared seven times this season for Wednesday, with his only league starts coming under caretaker manager Matt Hamshaw after Pedersen was dismissed, but he has been excluded from the last two matchday squads, with a whole host of other defenders ahead of him in the pecking order at Hillsborough.

With Weaver now out of the matchday squad, it will perhaps stall his development unless he can get minutes elsewhere - and it looks like that's set to happen.

According to The Wednesday Word, the Owls hierarchy are now set to sanction a temporary exit for Weaver, given the amount of options ahead of him, even though he was denied a loan move away last month due to an injury picked up by Di'Shon Bernard.

And it is London-based National League outfit Hornchurch that look likely to be the club that take 20-year-old Weaver on a short-term basis, with EFL clubs unable to do any deals other than for free agents until January 2027.

Promoted from the National League South earlier in the year, Hornchurch are performing well enough and sit 12th in the fifth tier standings, and if they can get a deal done for Weaver, then they'll be hoping he can bring his EFL experience into the fold and to push them up the table even further.

Given Wednesday's defensive options are mostly all fit and available again now, many Wednesday fans are seeing sense in Weaver's likely temporary departure.

Some supporters though are hopeful that Wednesday will be able to recall him if needed, given their luck recently with injuries.

Whilst some are potentially concerned that the young defender won't sign a new contract with the club if he isn't getting minutes - Weaver's current deal expires next summer.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#1997. ‘Not Manchester United standard’, Paul Merson raises concerns over Manchester United squad

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United have failed to hit the numbers expected off them after a lackluster campaign so far.

Michael Carrick was relieved off his duties after winning just 1 game in his first 10, while collecting only 8 points. Manchester United arr currently languishing in the relegation spots and Carrick’s successor, Mauricio Pochettino, has a massive task ahead.

Manchester United have been leaky in defence and haven’t gone a game without conceding a goal this season. Their attacking returns are equally disappointing with United failing to convert chances regularly.

Paul Merson believes Manchester United must strengthen their defence in January but insists their problems extend beyond the backline, with concerns over their midfield and attacking options also needing attention.

The January transfer window could be the first stop for Pochettino for some shopping but the budget given to him as per a previous report by readmanutd isn’t much to make a difference.

Paul Merson believes the club have several areas to improve rather than focusing only on their defence.

Speaking on Sky Sports, the former Arsenal midfielder made it clear that United need to bring in defensive reinforcements.

“Manchester United will have to get centre-halves in, defenders in and full-backs in,” Merson said.

However, Merson does not believe defensive recruitment alone will solve United’s problems. He also questioned the team’s ability to control games in midfield and expressed concerns about the quality of their attacking options.

“I wouldn’t say that’s just been the problem. I don’t think they’ve got legs in midfield, I don’t think they’re dominating games in midfield,” he explained.

He was also critical of United’s forward line, suggesting that the current attacking options are not consistently performing.

“I’ve never really been a massive fan of their front three. I think they’re not Manchester United standard, in my opinion.”

Merson also compared the current generation with some of the club’s former greats, including Wayne Rooney, Ruud van Nistelrooy, Roy Keane, Paul Scholes, David Beckham and Cristiano Ronaldo. He compared players’ consistency with those earlier.

“Back in the day when it’s Rooney and them kind of players and Van Nistelrooy and Keane and Scholes and Beckham and Ronaldo, they were seven, eight out of ten every week. There wasn’t a four out of ten and a nine out of ten.”

“And if they have a four the week after, it doesn’t really matter. So for me, it hasn’t just been the defence.”

United could face difficult decisions when the transfer window opens, particularly if they want to strengthen multiple areas of the squad and with the budget available to Pochettino, that doesn’t seem to be the case.

#1996. Senegal Knockout Tie Gives Chelsea A Double Xabi Alonso Audit

Chelsea’s World Cup watch has moved beyond simple minutes management.

Senegal’s Round-of-32 meeting with Belgium now gives Xabi Alonso a live read on two very different development tracks.

Nicolas Jackson’s attacking authority is the immediate question. Mamadou Sarr’s defensive readiness is the longer-term one.

Chelsea confirmed that Senegal kept their knockout hopes alive with a 5-0 win over Iraq, with Jackson featuring from the bench.

Senegal have since moved into the knockouts, where they face Belgium in Seattle on Wednesday 1 July.

Jackson and Sarr travel into that game with contrasting club questions attached. Both still carry clear Chelsea relevance.

Sarr has not been the loudest Chelsea story of the tournament.

That may actually make this test more useful.

The 20-year-old is still moving through the awkward stage between prospect, squad option and saleable BlueCo asset.

Knockout football against Belgium can sharpen that picture quickly.

The timing is awkward in the best possible way for Chelsea. Alonso steps into a squad with expensive centre-backs, academy-trained options and a board still comfortable using the market aggressively.

A disciplined Sarr performance would not end that search. It would give the recruitment team a stronger internal benchmark before committing another major fee.

Chelsea need defenders who can hold a high line, cover wide channels and still pass through pressure. Belgium should ask those questions more directly than most group-stage opponents.

The context matters. Chelsea’s recall note recorded that Sarr returned from Strasbourg after 18 appearances across Ligue 1 and the Conference League.

The club also noted that he had already earned his first Senegal cap.

That is a different profile from an academy player being carried by reputation alone.

There is a statistical base behind the interest too. When Chelsea completed the deal, beIN SPORTS noted that Sarr made 27 Ligue 1 appearances in his first Strasbourg season.

He helped them keep 10 clean sheets. He also produced a team-high 20 blocks and made 25 interceptions.

Those numbers explain why this Belgium game is not just a sentimental World Cup subplot.

Alonso’s Chelsea defence is already crowded with Levi Colwill, Wesley Fofana, Trevoh Chalobah and external targets still orbiting the plan.

ReadChelsea has already looked at why Colwill’s recovery story gives Alonso a defensive test. Sarr’s value is different.

He is still being evaluated as a physical, long-range defensive project.

Jackson’s role changes the editorial weight of the tie.

Chelsea’s striker picture has been messy for long enough. Any high-pressure international performance now carries wider meaning.

ReadChelsea has already framed the forward’s tournament as a live Senegal striker audit for Chelsea.

Belgium should stress both Chelsea questions at once.

Jackson has to offer penalty-box threat and transition security. Sarr, if trusted, has to defend space against a technically cleaner opponent.

He also has to show whether his recovery pace and frame translate under tournament pressure.

Sarr’s own mentality profile is worth noting. In a Chelsea World Cup Q&A, he named Lionel Messi, Sadio Mane and Paul Pogba as his tournament heroes.

His answer on Pogba focused on leadership and group mentality.

That lands neatly with the exact question Chelsea now need answered. Is there enough presence to go with the physical tools?

This is why Belgium feels like a pathway check rather than a routine World Cup watch item.

Chelsea do not need Sarr to solve the defence in July. They need clearer evidence on whether he belongs in Alonso’s first pre-season group.

He could need another loan. He could also become part of the club’s centre-back market arithmetic.

For Jackson, the question is more immediate. For Sarr, it is more structural.

Together, Senegal’s knockout tie gives Chelsea a rare clean look at two players on opposite ends of the same squad-building argument.

Who can help now, and who is worth protecting for later?

#1995. Michael Olise Gives Chelsea A Hard Xabi Alonso Wide-Player Benchmark

Michael Olise has moved from former Chelsea academy footnote to genuine Ballon d’Or conversation piece.

That should land at Cobham as more than a wistful what-if.

Bavarian Football Works relayed comments from former Chelsea and France winger Florent Malouda, who described the Bayern Munich forward as a live Ballon d’Or contender if France turn their World Cup run into silverware.

The point is not simply that Chelsea once had Olise in the building. It is that his rise provides a hard benchmark for the type of final-third specialist Xabi Alonso must either develop or buy.

Chelsea have spent heavily on attacking upside. Olise’s rise is a reminder that the real separator is not potential, but repeatable elite production.

Bayern’s own season review underlines why the conversation has accelerated.

The German champions confirmed Olise finished 2025/26 with 25 goals and 28 assists from 57 competitive appearances. He was also named Bayern’s Player of the Season for a second straight year, finishing ahead of Harry Kane and Luis Diaz in the fan vote.

That is elite production from a wide creator who does not play like a chalk-on-boots winger.

Olise can receive wide, drift inside, manipulate the half-space and still deliver the last pass at match-winning speed. Chelsea have bought attackers with pieces of that profile, but few have joined the dots with that level of consistency.

There is an obvious recruitment lesson here.

The market will now price that blend of creativity, ball security and goal threat close to superstar territory. If Chelsea want an Alonso attack that controls games rather than simply runs through them, the next winger decision cannot be judged on pace or upside alone.

It has to be judged on game control, final-third calm and repeat output.

The World Cup has sharpened the comparison.

Chelsea’s official France preview noted that Malo Gusto was in the same squad as N’Golo Kante and former Blues academy player Olise. It was a neat reminder of how many Chelsea strands sit inside Didier Deschamps’ group.

Bundesliga’s tournament analysis was even more revealing. It noted that Olise had reached 10 France goal involvements in 18 appearances and was named Player of the Match on his World Cup debut against Senegal.

That same analysis highlighted the tactical adjustment that moved Olise closer to Kylian Mbappe after half-time. His passing range then became the lever that changed the game.

That matters for Chelsea because Alonso’s best Bayer Leverkusen sides were built around players who could receive between lines without killing the tempo. Cole Palmer already gives Chelsea one version of that.

The wider question is whether the squad has another attacker who can bend matches from the opposite side without turning every possession into a one-v-one.

Olise’s Chelsea connection can easily become sentimental. The sharper editorial point is structural.

This is the calibre of player who once passed through the academy pathway and later became a global-level attacker elsewhere. Chelsea cannot change that history, but they can use it to stress-test the next wave of decisions.

That matters for Tyrique George, Kendry Paez, Estevao and any new wide signing.

ReadChelsea has already looked at how Tyrique George’s likely Everton return gives Alonso a fresh winger audit. Olise’s current standing raises the standard of that discussion.

He is no longer just a former academy name or a missed Premier League target. He is evidence of what happens when technical security, role clarity and patience meet elite coaching.

For Alonso, that is the real value of the Olise noise.

Chelsea do not need to turn every academy exit into regret. They do need to recognise the standard now being set by one of Cobham’s former pupils.

The next wide forward who gets serious minutes at Stamford Bridge has to be assessed against that ceiling, not against the safer language of potential.

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. Luke Shaw has returned to the Manchester United squad ahead of tonight’s Champions League fixture against Sporting in Lisbon.

The England international has missed the last eight matches in all competitions through injury. Shaw has not played since the 1-1 draw with Tottenham Hotspur at Old Trafford on 10 October. The 31-year-old trained with his team-mates at Carrington on Tuesday before being included in Mauricio Pochettino’s 22-man travelling squad.

Pochettino worked with Shaw during the early stages of the defender’s career at Southampton. Speaking at Tuesday’s press conference, the United head coach was reluctant to say whether the left-back would feature against Sporting.

“Obviously, it’s good to see him and he came from a small issue but now he needs to recover his best form,” Pochettino told the club’s official website. Lisandro Martinez started at left-back against Liverpool on Sunday before moving into central defence following Leny Yoro’s dismissal.

Goalkeeper Karl Darlow is also back in the squad, although Marcus Rashford, Carlos Baleba, Manuel Ugarte and Benjamin Sesko remain unavailable. Matheus Cunha is suspended following his red card against Roma.

United have six points from their first four Champions League fixtures, having beaten Sabah and Roma at Old Trafford. Wednesday’s match will be Pochettino’s first European fixture in charge of the club.

With Brentford visiting Old Trafford at the weekend, Pochettino has two opportunities this week to assess Shaw’s match fitness, should the defender be ready to play.
